statement: Full write flow of the hashtag page: whenever a post is published, the post service pushes a message to Kafka; that one message is consumed by a hashtag extractor, which extracts the hashtags from the caption and, for n hashtags, creates n entries in another Kafka partitioned by hashtag.
detail: The source of the flow is the post service, not the image service.
case_study: Hashtag page of the Instagram-like social network (hashtag service).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: if there are n hashtags, it creates n entries in this another Kafka, in which, it can be same Kafka, another topic.

statement: The second Kafka for hashtag entries can be the same Kafka cluster with another topic (post_hashtag); keeping it separate is about separation of concern. Each entry is a (hashtag, post) tuple and the topic is partitioned by hashtag.
case_study: Hashtag page of the Instagram-like social network (hashtag service).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: it can be same Kafka, another topic. But the idea is separation of concern. Post underscore hashtag

statement: Counting servers consume the hashtag-partitioned topic (e.g. three partitions, three servers); because all post-hashtag tuples of a particular hashtag go to the same server, the server can batch and do count += n on the database instead of count++, which makes this an efficient path.
case_study: Hashtag page of the Instagram-like social network (hashtag service).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: All post hashtag tuples go to the same server for a particular hashtag, you can efficiently batch and do count plus equal to n

statement: Kafka adapter pattern: the original post Kafka cannot be changed because search, notification and every other service depend on it, but the hashtag counting needs a different partitioning key; so you write an adapter - two Kafkas combined with a simple processor that only reorders or repartitions the messages. This is a very common practice.
case_study: Hashtag page of the Instagram-like social network (hashtag service).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It's a very common way to have two Kafka combined with a simple processor which just changes the order or repartitions.

statement: Read side of the hashtag page: hashtag API workers serve a normal GET request; on each request they read the entire hashtag document built for the page from the database and send it to the user.
case_study: Hashtag page of the Instagram-like social network (hashtag service).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Whenever the request comes, it talks to the database, gets this entire document that we just built.

statement: Because the hashtag page data does not change that frequently, put the hashtag API endpoint behind a CDN so the page renders immediately: users are served from the CDN instead of waiting relatively longer for a DB read, and the CDN takes care of geographic distribution.
case_study: Hashtag page of the Instagram-like social network (hashtag service).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: given that a lot of things would not change that frequently, you can put that endpoint behind the CDN.

statement: A CDN can cache JSON API responses, not only images: it caches whatever the origin sends and does not care whether it is an image, JSON or text.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: CDN, caching, JSON responses, not the images. At the end, whatever origin sends it, caches it.

statement: For the hashtag API, use either a CDN or a cache in front of it - pick your favorite; if you use a CDN you do not need the cache. The teacher would go for the CDN any day because the response is not changing.
case_study: Hashtag page of the Instagram-like social network (hashtag service).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I would go for CDN any day because the response is not changing.

statement: Freshness of the cached hashtag response: configure a TTL on the CDN (and/or explicitly invalidate when the top 100 photos or the count change); after the key expires the request goes to the API, which loads from the DB, and the result is cached and served again.
case_study: Hashtag page of the Instagram-like social network (hashtag service).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Add some TTL, do explicit invalidation over here.

statement: The popularity service built by the data science team notifies the hashtag service when it generates new top 100 photos for a hashtag by writing to their Kafka; the hashtag service consumes from that Kafka and writes the data into its own database. This stream is not very high throughput, so this is fine.
case_study: Hashtag page of the Instagram-like social network (hashtag service).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So what they do is they send it to their Kafka. We consume it from their Kafka.

statement: Even though the popularity service may store the top 100 photos in its own database, the hashtag service copies the data, formats and structures it its own way and stores it in its own database, to guarantee a very fast response time when the user opens the hashtag page.
case_study: Hashtag page of the Instagram-like social network (hashtag service).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: we are just copying the data and storing it over here because we want to guarantee very fast response time.

statement: A way almost every senior engineer works: to build any system well, understand what its read paths and write paths are and tackle one at a time.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: understand what your read path and write paths are and tackle one at a time.

statement: Every system discussed so far has some paths that write to the database and some paths that read from it; whenever you design or architect a system, pick one path and check whether it is heavily optimized.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You will always see there are some path that does the writing to the database and there are some path that read from the database.

statement: In the basic hashtag diagram, post service -> Kafka -> hashtag workers -> database is the write path, and the hashtag API reading from the database and serving it is the read path.
case_study: Hashtag page of the Instagram-like social network (hashtag service).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Now, this is where your write path is, where you're writing to the database. And this is where your read path is

statement: Read path optimization is the easy part: you typically add a cache and/or a CDN; check that you are doing enough so the read path has the bare minimum latency.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Read path is easy. You typically add cache and CDN to solve it.

statement: Once the read path is done, examine the write path step by step and ask whether each step does the bare minimum work: e.g. post service to Kafka should be a single API call - with two API calls you would need distributed transactions and ensuring consistency.
case_study: Hashtag page of the Instagram-like social network (hashtag service).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: If I have two API calls, then hey, what, I need to distribute transaction and ensuring consistency and whatnot.

statement: The number of workers you need to process from Kafka equals the number of partitions of the topic.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: the number of workers that you need to process from Kafka will be equal to the number of partitions that you have over here.

statement: On the write path into the database, check atomic updates and partial updates, whether the database is provisioned enough, and whether you are consuming at a decent enough pace - at every step ask if you are doing the bare minimum.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Atomic updates, partial updates and whatnot. Are you doing the bare minimum? Are you provisioning your database enough?

statement: Looking at the read path and the write path separately and tackling each one gives a very structured way to build robust systems; when you pick one path, think of the implementation and of what can go wrong.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It gives very structured way to build robust systems.

statement: When optimizing any path, think of the implementation at every single step - that is where most things are neglected; blow every component out of proportion (what if it gets a huge load?), fix it, and re-architect, one path at a time. This is what 'read path / write path optimization' means.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Thinking of implementation, making everything blow out of proportion and fixing it. One path at a time is the way to go.

statement: Read path of the hashtag API blown out of proportion: if one database gets high spikes, decide whether to partition it, whether you need replicas, add a cache to reduce the load on the database, and if that is not enough add a CDN in front of it.
case_study: Hashtag page of the Instagram-like social network (hashtag service).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: If that is not enough, add a CDN in front of it to do it.

statement: Write path thought through as an implementation: for a post with eight hashtags, the naive approach extracts eight hashtags from the caption and makes eight writes to the database; that is a lot of micro writes and not optimal, which is why you want batching.
case_study: Hashtag page of the Instagram-like social network (hashtag service).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I make eight writes onto this DB. Now I think about optimality. Is this good enough? Not really.

statement: To batch, everything for a particular hashtag must go to one server, so the hashtags are extracted and re-ingested into another Kafka partitioned by hashtag; that server batches and then writes to the database.
case_study: Hashtag page of the Instagram-like social network (hashtag service).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you extract the hashtag and then you re-ingest it into another Kafka by hashtag, where it is partitioned by hashtag.

statement: Takeaway: Kafka acts as glue in the hashtag design - the post Kafka feeds all other services (search, notification, feed), it is repartitioned to make the counting writes efficient, and the data science team interacts with the backend engineers through Kafka; everyone is decoupled and works at their own pace.
case_study: Hashtag page of the Instagram-like social network (hashtag service).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Everyone is decoupled. Everyone's working at their own speed pace.

statement: Takeaways also include the adapter pattern and effective batching and counting: the naive approach does count++ per event, which is not how a system works at scale - at every step find that pattern and fix it.
case_study: Hashtag page of the Instagram-like social network (hashtag service).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: because as part of naive, you will do count plus plus. That's not how a system works.

statement: Read path / write path optimization is almost a standard way to think about systems: think of what the read paths and the write paths are and tackle one at a time, because standard practice is to scale reads separately.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: because there's standard practice is to scale the read separately

statement: Next class continues social networks: implementing the image optimization service (this class showed how a CDN can be leveraged for it) and an interesting problem statement around message indicators.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: we'll be tomorrow implementing image optimization service. Today we saw how CDN, how we can leverage CDN to do that.

statement: The hashtag web server (read) and the asynchronous workers (write) were separated because they have different responsibilities - a web server versus asynchronous workers - not because read path and write path must live in separate services; read/write path is a way of approaching concerns, not a rule to split services.
detail: Raised by a student who understood the lecture as 'separate read and write paths into different services'.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: We did not separate it because it's read path and write path. We separated because they had different responsibilities.

statement: Partitions cannot match the number of hashtags: define n partitions, measure the throughput you get, and if it is too low, increase the number of partitions.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Basically, you define n partitions, you measure the throughput that you are getting. If you're getting less, you increase the number of partitions.

statement: Kafka partitioning (how messages are spread over partitions) was covered in depth in week 2 of the course.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: We, we went in depth of Kafka partitioning, what it happens, how it does that. Second week we talked about it.

statement: Each message in the hashtag-partitioned Kafka carries the hashtag and the post ID, so a counting server can group what it reads by hashtag even though one partition holds many different hashtags.
case_study: Hashtag page of the Instagram-like social network (hashtag service).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You will send in the message: this is the hashtag, this is the post ID.

statement: On the counting server, keep a hash table from hashtag to an integer starting at zero, do count++ for every message read, and once there is a big enough batch write the counts to the database.
case_study: Hashtag page of the Instagram-like social network (hashtag service).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: On the counting server side, have a hash table, do count plus plus and update map to count.

statement: Small implementation details like the per-hashtag hash table are something learners should work out themselves; the class cannot write every single line or spoon-feed everything.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This is very simple detail where I cannot literally write every single line over here.

statement: If the popularity service needs hashtag-level data, the data science team can consume the hashtag-partitioned Kafka (hashtag, post) themselves instead of rebuilding the same extraction; today the counting server is its only consumer, but data science might also start consuming it for their crunching.
detail: A student asked whether, if popularity is not hashtag-based, the popularity service would need its own adapter to get hashtags.
case_study: Hashtag page of the Instagram-like social network (hashtag service).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: If they need it, if they need it, they can consume it from here as well. They can listen to this Kafka.

statement: Redis Pub/Sub fit the chat design but not hashtag counting: chat needed real-time Pub/Sub, while here real-time is not needed; real-time Pub/Sub gives no persistence, whereas the counting service consumes at its own pace and the messages must persist.
detail: You still want a kind of Pub/Sub, but not real-time Pub/Sub. The student's framing: chat modeled each group membership as a Redis channel to pass messages between chat servers.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: There we needed real-time Pub/Sub. Here we don't need real-time. When it is real-time, it does not give you persistence.
flags: asr: [?a counting service is | asr: "accounting services"]

statement: With Redis Pub/Sub only the servers connected to Redis and subscribed to the channel at that moment get a message; if a counting server is down when the hashtag extractor sends, it never receives it and the message is discarded.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Whichever connection, whichever server is connected to Redis at that time, subscribe it to that channel, will get the message.

statement: The difference between Redis Pub/Sub and Kafka here is persistence and speed of consumption: Redis Pub/Sub is push based, so a very popular hashtag would keep bombarding one server, while Kafka consumers are pull based and consume (in batches) at their own pace.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: one of the server would keep on getting bombarded, because it's push based, not pull based.

statement: With real-time push the database speed also throttles consumption: the counting servers batch and write to the DB, so if the DB is overwhelmed writes take longer and incoming pushed messages overwhelm the servers even further.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So slowness of your database would also affect the rate of consumption.

statement: Redis Pub/Sub was used in the chat design because latency had to be minimal: messages had to be pushed to users rather than users pulling them.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: We wanted, because the latency had to be minimal. We had to push the messages to the user rather than users pulling it out

statement: Proposal: instead of a separate Kafka, the popularity service could call the hashtag API servers directly via webhooks, since top-100 updates are not frequent.
detail: The teacher called it a good approach but weighed the trade-off and preferred Kafka: the data science team would have to implement and manage the calls to your API, and if the hashtag API is down the update is lost and they will not reprocess it; work that does not need to be synchronous should be asynchronous.
case_study: Hashtag page of the Instagram-like social network (hashtag service).
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: if the popularity, this service directly call, like, use webhooks and directly call the API servers.

statement: Everything in computer science is a trade-off; you need to know what you are trading for what.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: everything in computer science is a trade-off. Now you need to know what you are trading, which things for what.

statement: With webhooks the data science team would have to implement and manage the code that calls your API; if the hashtag API is down they lose the update, and they will say reprocessing is not their job - writing to Kafka and being done is what they would prefer.
case_study: Hashtag page of the Instagram-like social network (hashtag service).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: They say, it's not our job. We'll write it to Kafka and done.

statement: Decouple as much as you can: anything that does not need to happen in real time in a synchronous way should not be done synchronously; the popularity update does not demand synchronicity and is a very nice use case for asynchronous consumption.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So you want to decouple as much as you can.

statement: When many updaters increment the same hashtag count, the database must provide atomicity; pick a database that gives atomic guarantees (a key feature to read about a database) - not only relational databases offer it; MySQL and DynamoDB both do.
detail: Raised for the NoSQL database chosen for the hashtag documents.
case_study: Hashtag page of the Instagram-like social network (hashtag service).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So you need to pick a database that gives you atomicity.

statement: The top-100 array in the hashtag document is most likely replaced wholesale: depending on what the data science team sends, they give a top hundred each time and you simply replace the entire array (no reading and re-sorting).
case_study: Hashtag page of the Instagram-like social network (hashtag service).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Most of all, it would give you a top hundred every time you go and replace our entire array.

statement: Partitioning the post Kafka by user ID does not mean one partition per user: it is one topic with many partitions, e.g. 1000 partitions for 1 million users, each partition handling about 1000 users.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: There is not one topic or rather one partition for each user ID.

statement: Kafka is not a single instance but a cluster; data is replicated, so if one node goes down another takes over - that is availability.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Kafka is a cluster. Cluster.
flags: check: ASR may have dropped "not" - contradicts the previous sentence
check: "rules up a system around" - wording unclear

statement: Kafka can go down: it gives about 99.9% availability, not four nines or five nines.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Kafka gives you 99.9% availability. It does not give you four, nine, five, nine availability.

statement: While Kafka is down, writes to it are lost. Three ways to handle it: if the data is critical, push to a dead letter queue and later consume and re-ingest into Kafka; if losing data is acceptable, drop it; or buffer it in memory for some time and write when Kafka comes back, else drop. Pick one depending on the system.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So either have a dead letter queue or lose the data or drop it in memory for some time.

statement: For this design the SLA is about how quickly you can consume messages from Kafka: Kafka's parallelism is proportional to the number of partitions, so measure the throughput, and if it does not fit the SLA increase the partitions and the workers.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: given the parallelism of Kafka is proportional to the number of partitions.

statement: Increasing partitions means choosing between online repartitioning and repartitioning with downtime, depending on how good your SRE team is; either way, have a strategy to scale things up.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: do have a strategy to scale this. You need to have a strategy to scale things up
flags: check: 'online repartitioning and partitioning that downtime' wording garbled

statement: Week 7 (Sunday), on the distributed task scheduler, covers how SLAs define a system and how to ensure they are met; this discussion is a precursor.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: In seventh week, Sunday, when we discuss distributed task scheduler, we'll understand how SLA defines our system

statement: A student framed SLA thinking via component state: Kafka and the DB are stateful, workers and servers are stateless; stateless servers are sized by load testing for QPS, while a stateful component going down means downtime or data loss, so the question is what to do when stateful things go down.
detail: The teacher did not comment on the classification; his answer was to look up dead letter queues.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: So state means Kafka is stateful, DB is stateful and rest all the workers or servers are stateless.

statement: You do not always have to add yet another component (such as a dead letter queue); sometimes it is fine to lose some data.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you don't always have to add, add another, yet another component. It's sometimes it's okay to lose the data.

statement: When data cannot be lost at all, the system must be highly available: e.g. Uber's SOS emergency system (teacher's YouTube video) - if something bad happens in a cab and you press SOS, the service cannot be down and no message or data may be lost.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It's very important for SOS system to be up and running.

statement: Very few systems give 100% uptime guarantees; with leader-replica databases you have to bear a failover of a couple of seconds (two, three seconds) when the leader goes down.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Very few system give you a hundred percent uptime guarantees.

statement: Proposal: use leaderless replication to avoid leader-failover downtime. The teacher's answer: possible, but it brings another complexity - multi-master replication (and, as the student added, conflict resolution); you get some, you lose some.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: If you don't want, but then that has another complexity, multi-master replication.

statement: Kafka keeps messages forever unless a deletion policy is configured, e.g. periodically deleting messages older than 30 days.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: On Kafka messages will be there forever unless you have configured a deletion policy.

statement: Horizon: with a deletion policy, the time at which the last deletion ran; consumers cannot read messages beyond it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: the time at which the last deletion ran, that's your horizon time and that you cannot read messages beyond that.

statement: Reading from the horizon in Kafka or Kinesis means reading from the beginning of the stream - which is not necessarily the first ever message, since older messages may have been deleted by the deletion policy.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: beginning does not mean the first ever message because it could be very well possible that those messages are deleted

statement: Checkpointing: after reading a set of messages a consumer commits to Kafka, which marks that this consumer ID has committed up to this message; the consumer can later ask Kafka to read from the last checkpoint (last commit).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: it marks on Kafka that this consumer at this ID as committed to this message.

statement: Consumers keep committing to Kafka periodically; if a consumer crashes after consuming some messages, on restart it can resume from the horizon or from the last checkpoint - resuming from the last checkpoint reprocesses the messages consumed since that commit.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So you periodically keep on committing to Kafka.
flags: check: speaker - Student 4 may already be speaking in this turn

statement: Three places a Kafka consumer can start: the horizon, the last checkpoint, or the current (latest) message. A brand-new consumer (e.g. adding a search service to an existing Kafka) starts from the horizon; an existing consumer that crashed resumes from the last checkpoint; if losing data is fine, start from the current message.
detail: How far back to go is use-case specific; exceptions exist.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So these are three possible ways to do it. Horizon, last checkpoint or whatever the current is.

statement: Retention length has a big impact: no deletion policy means data forever and a large amount of storage; a low-throughput system can afford to keep its data, but with huge volume at high throughput a long retention period blows up your disk, so you typically set deletion policies.
detail: Asked as: keeping data six months versus 30 days - is that a big difference? Teacher: big difference.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: if you have huge amount of data flowing at very high throughput, then having a longer retention period means your disk will blow up.

statement: To keep historical data of a high-volume Kafka, have a consumer read the old events, archive them to S3 and then delete them from Kafka; Kafka now also has plugins that archive a batch of events to S3, Blob Storage or GCS before triggering deletion.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: before deleting it, it takes a bunch of events and archives it to S3 or Blob Storage or GCS

statement: In most cases consumers resume from the last checkpoint; new consumers start from the horizon; very few cases start from the most recent message.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I've seen very few cases doing from here. Very few. Most do this for the last checkpoint.

statement: Question framing: a pod benchmarked at 400 requests per second needs three servers for 1000 rps; to grow, should you add servers or find the bottleneck and raise per-server capacity? This boils down to horizontal versus vertical scalability, assuming the stateful dependency (e.g. S3) can handle the load.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: They're just talking about either horizontal scalability or vertical scalability.

statement: Scaling out the servers that generate pre-signed URLs only helps if the stateful component they depend on (S3) can handle the increased requests; the teacher assumes it can.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: One thing when you're scaling up, I'm assuming that your S3s can handle the request.

statement: Adding servers versus optimizing is first a management decision on engineering cost: companies with decent money in the bank often throw money at AWS for more machines rather than spend engineers' time optimizing, because two more servers are typically very cheap compared with engineer salaries.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: typically throwing money at AWS, getting two more servers is very cheap as compared to salaries of engineers.

statement: If the company wants to keep the same servers and get the max out of them, the only way is application-level profiling (New Relic, Datadog or an OpenTelemetry system): not just CPU or memory percentage, but for an HTTP call that invokes a handler which calls, say, 5,000 functions, it tells how much time each took so you find the bottleneck.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: the only way to do it is by profiling the application
flags: check: "not active profiling" may be the student answering

statement: Application-level profiling is costly - in money paid to profiling tools, in data, and in response time, since it captures the time of every function call - so you do not turn it on for all production machines, only on a canary or a few machines.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you may not turn on application level profiling for all of the production grade systems, but on a canary machine

statement: Profile in production by splitting it (e.g. 90/10) behind a load balancer that routes round robin or by another strategy, and monitor the 10% instances with application profiling; you take a response-time hit for a while but learn which function takes how much time and find the bottleneck.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: And you monitor those 10% instances using application profiling.

statement: Measure before optimizing: without measurement you only assume what takes time; with data you can drill down to the exact function taking the most time and optimize it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: unless you have it measured, you can just assume that, oh, this might be taking time

statement: New Relic and Datadog are the market leaders in application profiling, New Relic the biggest; the teacher named Nagios as the open-source alternative.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: New Relic, Datadog, these two are market leaders at the moment. New Relic is the biggest one out there and open source alternative is Nagios.

statement: For a Python stack, cProfile is a simple option: text-based output that is still decent enough to show which function takes most time. The teacher used it recently on his local machine, never in production.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: If you are into Python, check out cProfile, that would give you a text based output, but it's still decent enough.

statement: Instagram uses cProfile in production on one of their servers and has a blog post about it.

verbatim: Instagram uses cProfile in production on one of their servers. They have a blog on it

statement: More RAM or more CPU to serve more requests: throwing more of either generally helps, but adding one may not - e.g. a CPU-heavy encryption/decryption workload gains nothing from more RAM. Understand your workload: of the four resources (CPU, memory, network, disk), see which one you use most and add more of that.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: At the end, you have four things. As I always say, CPU, memory, network and disk.

statement: For a Go server doing lots of parallel work in goroutines, add CPU first so more goroutines can be scheduled; then, depending on what the goroutines do, add RAM - e.g. if each goroutine holds about 20 MB, supporting more goroutines needs that extra memory.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: CPU, right? Because you need more CPU so that it can schedule large number of goroutines there.

statement: Do not store all 1 million images in the hashtag document: they will never all be scrolled, so keep just the first page in the document.
case_study: Hashtag page of the Instagram-like social network (hashtag service).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So it makes no sense for you to store it within the document. Just the first page.

statement: Proposal: just for counting, an in-memory distributed queue would do instead of a persistent Kafka, accepting the loss of a minute of data on a crash. Teacher: then you are doing exactly the same thing; RabbitMQ is fine, Kafka is fine - what you are using is a partitioned message broker.
case_study: Hashtag page of the Instagram-like social network (hashtag service).
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: If you are using RabbitMQ, that's also fine. Kafka also it's fine, and then what you are doing is you are using a partitioned...

statement: Kafka is not used here just to count: the persisted information can be picked up by other services too.
case_study: Hashtag page of the Instagram-like social network (hashtag service).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You are not doing it for persistent just to count valuable information. It can be picked by other services

statement: Why not use Kafka to hold data like a database or S3? Access pattern: you need transactional properties, which a database has and Kafka does not, and lookups such as getting a post by ID are not possible on Kafka.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Access pattern, access pattern, you need transactional properties. Kafka does not give you that, database has transaction properties.

statement: Kafka is always a message broker and should never be your source of truth - you can, but you should not.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: No, Kafka is always a message broker. It can never be your source of truth. You can, but you should not.

statement: Kafka as the first point of entry: in massive analytics ingestion such as Google Analytics or YouTube watch-time analytics, every incoming event hits the API server, which pushes it to Kafka; it is then aggregated, processed and stored in specialized databases.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This is where your Kafka becomes a first point of entry rather than a persistent database.

statement: With high-volume, high-rate ingestion you do not write directly to the database (it might cry, and you may not yet know how to structure the data - that is determined afterwards for analytics); accept the write in an API server, put it into Kafka and process it asynchronously.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: High ingestion, high volume. Okay, because then you don't know what the structure of your data

statement: The usual pattern is the other way around: store in the database first, then push an event onto Kafka; Kafka-first is the exception for high-volume ingestion.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Because everywhere you see the other way around. And I'm storing it in database and then I push an event onto Kafka.

statement: The teacher has built a bunch of analytics systems; in all of them events were ingested into Kinesis (not Kafka) first and consumed from there - first accept the users' writes, then figure out what to do with them.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I've built bunch of analytics system, everywhere we ingested in Kinesis, not Kafka, and then from there we consumed it.

statement: Kafka does not provide a dead letter queue; use, say, RabbitMQ or SQS (which do) as the dead letter queue - if the write to Kafka fails, write to that other queue, assuming it is up; SQS fits really well.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You have, let's say, RabbitMQ or an SQS as your dead letter queue for that.

statement: Proposal: instead of a separate queue, write the failed message into our own database. Teacher: that is the transaction outbox pattern - write to the DB what you wanted to write but could not, and process it later.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: Basically transaction outbox pattern is what you are talking about.

statement: Think of MapReduce (Spark jobs, Hadoop MapReduce jobs) as distributed computing: the counting servers - normal stateless VMs consuming from Kafka - could be replaced by a Spark cluster, which has Kafka connectors and would do the count++ and batch writes to the database; how you implement it is up to you.
case_study: Hashtag page of the Instagram-like social network (hashtag service).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You can also replace this with a Spark cluster. It would work just fine because Spark has Kafka connectors

statement: All these frameworks do distributed computing: one machine is not enough to compute everything, so you do it in a distributed way; pick one of Kafka, Kinesis, Flume, Flink and so on. The teacher uses the generic name 'counting servers' to avoid picking one tool from the massive ecosystem.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: One machine is not enough to compute everything. You want to do it in a distributed way.

statement: To learn data engineering, start with Spark using the O'Reilly book on Spark ('Effective Spark' is mostly the name); first learn to use it, then go into its internals. Spark is mind-blowingly awesome, has its own flaws, and you should definitely know at least Spark.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Start with Spark. Start with a book for effective Spark. The O'Reilly book.
flags: check: book title - teacher unsure ('mostly the name of the book')

statement: MapReduce is a computing paradigm; Hadoop MapReduce is easy to learn; start with Spark and then venture into Flume, Flink and others.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: basically MapReduce is a computing paradigm, but you can learn Hadoop MapReduce very easily.

statement: Implement what you learn: without implementation it is all theoretical knowledge, because the problems only appear when you implement. The teacher took on big data leadership with no prior idea about it, learned by doing, and is now optimizing Spark.
